cells.tense: You are here with the pen, tending what is still small and letting it grow.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Set down something you've been keeping open for someone as finished, not as a failure. Then rest your hands.
cells.core:
When you know what deserves your attention, you tend it the way a gardener tends a bed: enough, on time, without pulling the stems to hurry them. The ones near you grow because they aren't being managed, and they feel the difference. That's rarer than it sounds. You can watch something change and keep your hands still, and it gets to arrive at its own pace.

Notice what's finishing now. It might be something you've held wide open a long while — a decision, a person, a habit that mattered. The skill here isn't holding on harder. Let it close on purpose and see what your hands feel like without it. Rest can look like nothing for a day. What's left standing is what actually grew while you watched.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing and don't pull it to hurry.
cells.verb: Tending what needs to grow without forcing it
cells.place: Where you know what to attend to before you can explain why

cells.tense: You are already reaching into a future that isn't yours to arrange and calling it care.
cells.act: take the next step with only enough light for that step
cells.ask: Some future you're gripping: take one small step on it with only the light you have, then stop and leave part of the road dark.
cells.core:
Where you know what to attend to, worry has taken over the watching. You can feel exactly what needs care before anyone says it, and that knowing has tilted into getting ahead of what you're caring for. A person is mid-sentence and you're already arranging their next week. They might feel managed in a way that's hard to name. What you give is real; the timing isn't theirs anymore.

You can't plan your way into trust. Picture one situation you're gripping a year from now, going fine, and keep that picture without a script for getting there. Then take a single step toward it, whatever the light allows, and stop. Part of the road stays dark. The grip thinks it's love. Loosen it and see what's still cared for.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already closed behind you.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: There's something that pulls you and you've gone quiet about it. Step toward it once — a look, a note, a first move — for no reason but that it pulls.
cells.core:
The instinct to tend what's small is in you, but here there's no bed in view — no person, no project, nothing growing under your hands. You might look like someone fine on their own, and part of you keeps score that way. What you want has gone quiet too, so there's nothing to steer by. It isn't that you stopped wanting. The field you usually water isn't here to water.

Don't strain to feel something that isn't there. Let yourself want it plainly, just to yourself, and then face it — a small step, real, toward a light you actually chose. Not because it's owed. Knowing what matters follows moving toward it. Step first; the rest catches up.

cells.tense: You are holding the shape of care for people who never asked, and feeling emptied by it.
cells.act: stop holding what no longer serves
cells.ask: Pick a habit of care you keep for someone out of course, and stop carrying it. Don't explain. Watch what your hands do with the room it leaves.
cells.core:
You've become the one who tends things here without ever deciding to. Other people call you the caretaker, and you feel like someone running low. When you describe what you've kept going, it sounds like nothing anyone asked for. They hand you things to carry and keep expecting you to have the room.

Stop holding one arrangement you've kept upright past its use — a habit, a role, a thing you mind so it doesn't fall over. Set it down on your end. Don't announce it. What it leaves is the honest part: lighter than you'd guess, and more yours. Tend what's yours once the borrowed arrangements sit down.
cells.sheetLine: Others call you the carer. You're someone running low.

attempts.check: The draft's riskiest claim is that the person experiences some of the care as roles they never chose; the record supports depletion and being seen as caretaker, not that the roles were imposed from outside. A reasonable reader could say the caring is chosen and they simply haven't spoken about the cost. The ask survives being wrong: stopping one held thing and noticing what's left works whether the role was taken on or handed over. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person would be any line implying they must have had a deprived childhood to be like this; it's cut.
